content: 1. The study conducted by Japaridze et al. focused on decentralizing hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing to harm reduction sites in Georgia, as part of the HEAD-START initiative. This approach aimed to improve access to testing and care for individuals at high risk of HCV infection. 2. Huang et al. implemented a strategy to scale up the in-hospital care cascade for hepatitis C virus in Taiwan. Their work emphasized the importance of integrating molecular diagnostics and clinical care to enhance treatment outcomes. 3. Howes et al. explored clinical care pathways for patients with hepatitis C, identifying and addressing critical barriers to effective treatment. Their findings highlighted the need for streamlined processes to improve patient outcomes. 4. Hirsch et al. evaluated a multicomponent quality improvement intervention designed to enhance the efficiency of hepatitis C screening and diagnosis. Their study demonstrated the potential for systematic approaches to improve care delivery. 5. Hellard et al. investigated community-based point-of-care hepatitis C testing and general practitioner-initiated direct-acting antiviral therapy in Yangon, Myanmar. The CT2 study provided insights into the feasibility and effectiveness of decentralized care models. 6. Hamid et al. examined the lower age limit for hepatitis C screening in large elimination programs targeting highly endemic areas. Their findings contributed to optimizing screening strategies for maximum impact. 7. The London Joint Working Group on Substance Use and Hepatitis C published findings in 2020, emphasizing the importance of collaborative efforts to address HCV among individuals with substance use disorders. 8. Ford et al. implemented universal screening for hepatitis C virus in emergency departments using a best practice advisory system. Their study demonstrated the feasibility and benefits of integrating HCV screening into acute care settings. 9. Coyle et al. shared lessons learned from integrating routine HCV testing in primary care settings across five federally qualified health centers in Philadelphia. Their work highlighted the importance of embedding HCV care into primary care workflows. 10. Chang et al. conducted a village-to-village screening program for hepatitis B and C in remote communities using quantitative HBsAg and anti-HCV testing with reflex HCV core antigen tests. This population-based prospective cohort study provided valuable data on the effectiveness of community-based screening. 11. Casas et al. piloted the implementation of reflex testing for active hepatitis C virus infection diagnosis at two healthcare centers. Their findings underscored the potential for reflex testing to streamline diagnostic pathways. 12. Casas et al. also reported on the implementation of reflex testing in Andalusia as part of efforts to eliminate hepatitis C. Their study highlighted the role of reflex testing in improving care cascades. 13. Calner et al. analyzed HCV screening, linkage to care, and treatment patterns across various sites within an academic medical center. Their findings provided insights into site-specific challenges and opportunities for improving care delivery. 14. Butsashvili et al. presented preliminary findings on integrating hepatitis C treatment with harm reduction services in Georgia. Their work demonstrated the feasibility and benefits of combining these services to address HCV among high-risk populations. 15. Bielen et al. evaluated the appropriateness of screening baby boomers for hepatitis C in emergency departments in Belgium. Their study contributed to the ongoing discussion on targeted screening strategies. 16. Averhoff et al. reviewed the progress and challenges of a pioneering hepatitis C elimination program in Georgia. Their findings highlighted the importance of sustained efforts and innovative strategies in achieving elimination goals. 17. Patel et al. reported on the outcomes of hepatitis C birth-cohort testing and linkage to care at selected U.S. sites. Their study emphasized the importance of targeted screening for improving care cascades. 18. Mera et al. described the identification and clinical management of individuals with chronic hepatitis C virus infection within the Cherokee Nation. Their work provided a model for integrating HCV care into community health systems. 19. Janjua et al. analyzed the population-level cascade of care for hepatitis C in British Columbia, Canada, using the BC Hepatitis Testers Cohort. Their findings offered valuable insights into care gaps and opportunities for improvement. 20. Ndagijimana et al. evaluated one-stop TB-HIV services in Rwanda, comparing cohorts from 2001–2005 and 2006–2010. Their study highlighted the benefits of integrated care models for co-infected patients. 21. Gamell et al. examined the prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV using the Option B+ cascade in rural Tanzania. The One Stop Clinic model demonstrated the potential for integrated care to improve maternal and child health outcomes.
